title: Generalization and PAC intuition
summary: Use population risk, empirical risk, and PAC language to explain why a low training error is not enough.
objectives: Read PAC as an accuracy-confidence statement

sections.title: Lecture core · Generalization gap
sections.body: The lecture distinction is simple but essential: empirical risk measures observed examples, while population risk measures the distribution of future examples. A low training error is evidence about the sample; it becomes evidence about the population only under assumptions about sampling, model capacity, and stability.

math.explanation: Subtract the observed-sample risk from the population risk for the same hypothesis. The gap is not a constant property of an algorithm: it depends on the data distribution, sample size, hypothesis class, and evaluation protocol.

symbols.meaning: empirical risk on the observed sample

math.name: Generalization gap formula
math.purpose: Use it to make the generalization gap claim operational; state its assumptions before applying it.

sections.title: Textbook depth · PAC language
sections.body: A PAC-style statement says that, with high probability over the training sample, the learned hypothesis has population error at most $\varepsilon$. $\varepsilon$ controls the allowed error and $\delta$ controls the probability that the guarantee fails. Therefore the confidence level is $1-\delta$; never swap the roles of $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$.

math.explanation: Read the statement from inside out: the learned model's population risk is at most $\varepsilon$, and this claim holds with confidence $1-\delta$ over the random training sample.

symbols.meaning: population risk of the fitted hypothesis

math.name: PAC language formula
math.purpose: Use it to make the pac language claim operational; state its assumptions before applying it.

sections.title: Lecture core · What breaks the estimate?
sections.body: The basic train–test story assumes the examples are independent and identically distributed. Duplicates, leakage, time drift, and distribution shift can make a validation score look precise while answering the wrong question. Always state the evaluation population before trusting a number.

sections.title: Reference boundary · Optional theory
sections.body: The learning-theory reference develops agnostic PAC and sample-complexity results beyond the current short lesson. Use it to understand why capacity and sample size affect confidence, but keep the current lecture syllabus as the exam boundary.

examples.title: Worked example: read a PAC statement
steps: Suppose a statement uses $\varepsilon=0.05$ and $\delta=0.10$. The allowed population error is $5\%$.
The failure probability is $10\%$, so the confidence is $1-\delta=0.90$, or $90\%$.
The statement does not say that 90% of future predictions are correct on every run; it describes the probability of the guarantee over sampled training sets.
examples.answer: Translate $\varepsilon$ as accuracy/error tolerance and $\delta$ as the probability the guarantee fails.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Does a smaller empirical risk guarantee a smaller population risk?
criticalQuestions.angle: State the missing assumptions rather than answering from the training score alone.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: No. The guarantee requires conditions relating the sample, hypothesis class, and distribution; flexible models can have low empirical risk and poor generalization.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What changes when train and test data are not identically distributed?
criticalQuestions.angle: Ask which probability distribution appears in empirical risk and which appears in deployment risk.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The basic IID PAC interpretation no longer applies directly; the evaluation must model distribution shift or use a target-domain sample.
